tool.name: LightGBM
tool.tagline: Fast, memory-efficient gradient boosting with leaf-wise trees
tool.description: LightGBM is Microsoft's gradient boosting framework, built for speed and large datasets. It grows trees leaf-wise on histogram-binned features, handles categorical features and missing values natively, and supports classification, regression, ranking and custom objectives. With a scikit-learn compatible API and a native API, it is a go-to choice for tabular data from Kaggle to production.

glossary.def: One of the value ranges a feature is cut into before training (at most 255 by default). LightGBM only tries split points between bins, which makes finding splits much faster.
Growing a tree by always splitting the single leaf that reduces the loss the most, wherever it is. Fits better for the same number of leaves but can make deep, lopsided trees.
Growing a tree by splitting every leaf at one depth before going deeper, so the tree stays balanced. Used by most other tree libraries.
One step of gradient boosting, in which one more tree is added (one per class for multi-class problems). The number of rounds is the number of trees.
A score for predicted probabilities that punishes confident mistakes hard: predicting 99% for something that turns out false costs far more than predicting 60%. Lower is better.
LightGBM's trained model in its native interface: all the trees plus their settings. The scikit-learn style classes keep one in their booster_ attribute.
In LightGBM, training each tree on a random share of the rows. It only happens when both subsample < 1 and subsample_freq > 0.
A way of writing a probability p as log(p / (1 - p)): 0 means 50%, positive means more likely yes, negative more likely no. The sigmoid turns it back into a probability.
In LightGBM, the loss it minimises while training, chosen by a name such as "regression", "binary" or "poisson".
A choice of loss for counts, such as visits per day or claims per year: it assumes the counts vary around an average that is never negative.
A choice of loss for amounts that are often exactly zero and otherwise positive, such as insurance claims per customer.
A range a model gives for a single prediction that the true value should fall in a stated share of the time, such as 90%.
Training a model to put items in the best order for each search or user, rather than predicting a number or class for each item on its own.
In ranking, one search or one user visit that comes with a list of candidate items to put in order. Items are only compared with others from the same query.
A ranking objective that learns from pairs of items in the same query, pushing hardest on pairs whose swap would change the top of the list most. LightGBM's default for ranking.
A ranking score from 0 to 1, where 1 is the perfect order. Mistakes near the top cost more than mistakes lower down; NDCG@10 looks only at the first 10 positions.
How much each relevance level is worth in NDCG. LightGBM's default, 2^label - 1, makes a perfect match (4) worth far more than a fair one (2).
A boosting mode that, in each round, temporarily leaves out some existing trees (dropout) so new trees can't lean on them. Sometimes more accurate, but slower and unreliable with early stopping.
Gradient-based One-Side Sampling: each round keeps all rows the model still gets badly wrong, samples the rest and gives the sampled ones extra weight, to train faster on big data.
A tree whose leaves each hold a small linear model instead of a single number, so predictions can change smoothly inside a leaf.
LightGBM's trick of packing several mostly-zero columns that are never non-zero in the same row into one column, each using its own range of bins.
The second derivative of the loss: how quickly its slope (the gradient) changes as a prediction moves. Boosting libraries use it to decide how big each leaf's correction should be.
The plain sum of a boosted model's tree outputs, before it is turned into a prediction. For a yes/no classifier it is the log-odds, which the sigmoid turns into a probability.
The function that turns a model's raw score into the prediction you see: the sigmoid for probabilities, or exp for counts (a log link).
A processor feature that makes one physical core appear as two logical cores. It helps some workloads, but number-crunching libraries usually run best with one thread per physical core.
NVIDIA's system for running general calculations on its GPUs. device_type="cuda" tells LightGBM to train on an NVIDIA GPU.
An older, vendor-neutral system for running calculations on GPUs from different makers; LightGBM's device_type="gpu" uses it.
Apache Spark: a system for processing very large datasets by splitting the work across many machines in a cluster.
Microsoft's open-source library for running machine learning, including LightGBM, on Spark clusters.

concepts.name: LightGBM with the scikit-learn API
concepts.summary: Train LGBMClassifier and LGBMRegressor like any scikit-learn estimator.
concepts.why: The scikit-learn-style classes get you a strong model for tables of data in a few lines, and scikit-learn's tools work with them.
concepts.body:
A single decision tree is easy to read but rarely very accurate. **Gradient boosting** gets accuracy through teamwork: it builds trees one after another, and each new tree is trained to fix the mistakes the trees before it still make. To predict, it adds up the outputs of all the trees. Like students correcting homework in turn, each one only fixes what is still wrong.

LightGBM, made by Microsoft, is a gradient boosting library built for speed on large tables of data. The `lightgbm` package gives you estimators that behave like scikit-learn's:

- `LGBMClassifier` for classification, with two classes or more,
- `LGBMRegressor` for regression,
- `LGBMRanker` for putting items in order, such as search results (a later lesson).

The usual pattern applies: hyperparameters in the constructor, then `fit(X, y)`, `predict`, `predict_proba` and `score`, and scikit-learn's tools for splitting, scoring and comparing models accept them. X can be a NumPy array or a pandas DataFrame, whose column names are kept.

Defaults: 100 trees (`n_estimators`), a **learning rate** of 0.1 (how much each new tree may change the prediction; smaller steps need more trees) and at most 31 leaves per tree (`num_leaves`, explained in the next lesson). No feature scaling is needed, because a tree only compares values with cut-offs, and missing values (`NaN`) are allowed. Class labels may even be text: the classifier converts them itself and lists them in `classes_`.

While training, LightGBM prints warnings such as "No further splits with positive gain", meaning no split would improve that tree any more. Pass `verbose=-1` to the constructor to silence them once you know what they mean.

Its main selling point is **speed**. Before training, LightGBM sorts each feature's values into a limited number of ranges, called **bins**, and then only tries split points between bins. Together with the way it grows trees, this often makes it several times faster than other boosting libraries on large data, with similar accuracy.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)

model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(round(model.score(X_te, y_te), 3))           # 0.944
print(model.predict_proba(X_te.iloc[:2]).round(3))
# [[0. 1.]
#  [1. 0.]]

labels = y_tr.map({0: "malignant", 1: "benign"})    # string labels work too
print(lgb.LGBMClassifier(verbose=-1).fit(X_tr, labels).classes_)  # ['benign' 'malignant']
takeaways: Gradient boosting builds trees one after another, each fixing the earlier trees' mistakes
LGBMClassifier/LGBMRegressor follow scikit-learn's fit/predict pattern
No scaling needed; NaN and text class labels are fine
`verbose=-1` silences training warnings
pitfalls: Silencing warnings with verbose=-1 before ever reading them; they often reveal data problems.

quiz.q: Which of these does LightGBM's LGBMClassifier accept without extra preprocessing?
quiz.explain: The classifier converts text labels to numbers internally and lists them in classes_.

quiz.q: Why does LightGBM sort feature values into bins before training?
options: So it only has to try a few hundred split points per feature, which is much faster
To turn numbers into categories for the user
quiz.explain: Trying cut points only between bins, not between every pair of distinct values, makes finding splits fast.

concepts.name: Leaf-wise growth and num_leaves
concepts.summary: See how LightGBM grows trees leaf by leaf, and control their size with num_leaves, max_depth and min_child_samples.
concepts.why: num_leaves is LightGBM's most important parameter, and it behaves differently from max_depth in other libraries.
concepts.body:
Picture growing a tree one split at a time. Most tree libraries grow **level-wise**: they split every leaf at one depth before going deeper, so the tree stays balanced, like filling in a family tree one generation at a time. LightGBM grows **leaf-wise**: at each step it splits whichever single leaf reduces the loss the most, wherever it is in the tree.

For the same number of leaves, leaf-wise growth fits the data better. The catch is that it can build deep, lopsided trees, with one very long branch, that overfit small datasets.

So how complicated the model can get is controlled mainly by:

- `num_leaves` (default 31): the most leaves one tree may have. This is the key setting. A balanced tree d levels deep has up to 2^d leaves, so 31 leaves is about the size of depth 5, but shaped very differently. When you set both, keep `num_leaves` below `2^max_depth`.
- `max_depth` (default -1, no limit): an extra guard against very deep branches, useful on small data.
- `min_child_samples` (also called `min_data_in_leaf`, default 20): the fewest training rows a leaf may hold. Raising it (50-500 for large data) is one of the most effective ways to curb overfitting.
- `min_split_gain` (default 0): how much a split must reduce the loss to be made at all.

Together with `learning_rate` and `n_estimators`, these settings decide most of the model's behaviour. A typical start for medium-sized data: `num_leaves` 15-63, `min_child_samples` 20-100, `learning_rate` 0.05, and early stopping (a later lesson) to pick the number of trees.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=5000, n_features=10, noise=10, random_state=0)

for params in [dict(num_leaves=31),
               dict(num_leaves=31, max_depth=5),
               dict(num_leaves=31, min_child_samples=300)]:
    m = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=50, verbose=-1, **params).fit(X, y)
    t = m.booster_.trees_to_dataframe()          # one row per tree node
    leaves = t[t["left_child"].isna()]          # rows with no children are leaves
    avg_leaves = leaves.groupby("tree_index").size().mean()
    print(params, round(avg_leaves, 1), int(leaves["node_depth"].max()) - 1)
# {'num_leaves': 31} 31.0 14                    (31 leaves, but 14 levels deep: lopsided)
# {'num_leaves': 31, 'max_depth': 5} 27.3 5      (depth cap limits the branches)
# {'num_leaves': 31, 'min_child_samples': 300} 13.0 12  (big leaves stop splitting early)
takeaways: Trees grow leaf-wise: always split the leaf that helps most
`num_leaves` is the main size control; keep it below 2^max_depth
Raise `min_child_samples` to fight overfitting
pitfalls: Copying max_depth=6 from another library's settings and leaving num_leaves=31, then wondering why trees behave differently.

quiz.q: Your LightGBM model overfits a small dataset. Which change is most directly helpful?
quiz.explain: Fewer leaves and more samples per leaf limit how finely the trees can fit noise.

concepts.name: Categorical features and missing values
concepts.summary: Use pandas category columns so LightGBM splits on categories directly, and let it handle NaN without filling gaps.
concepts.why: Built-in handling is faster and often more accurate than one-hot encoding or filling in missing values.
concepts.body:
**Categorical features.** One-hot encoding turns a column such as city into one 0/1 column per city, which gets unwieldy with hundreds of cities. LightGBM can split on such a column directly. At each split it lines the categories up by how much their rows push the prediction up or down, then finds the best place to cut that line into two groups: say Oslo and Rome on one side, every other city on the other.

There are two ways to mark a column as categorical:

- give it the pandas `category` type with `df[col].astype("category")`; LightGBM notices it automatically,
- or pass `categorical_feature=["city", ...]` (names or positions) to `fit`; those columns must hold whole numbers 0 or above.

The model remembers the categories it saw. When predicting, give the column the same list of categories, as the code does with `pd.Categorical(..., categories=...)`. Categories with very few rows are easy to overfit: `min_data_per_group` (default 100) and `cat_smooth` make LightGBM more careful with them. With many rare categories, it can also help to merge them into one "other" category first.

**Missing values.** Many models refuse rows with `NaN`, so you would first fill each gap with a stand-in such as the column's average. That is called **imputation**, and LightGBM doesn't need it: each split learns which side rows with a missing value should go to. So don't fill gaps by reflex. The fact that a value is missing can itself be useful information.

`zero_as_missing=True` makes LightGBM treat zeros as missing too, for data where 0 really means unknown. Text (`object`) columns are refused; convert them with `astype("category")`.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
df = pd.DataFrame({"store": rng.choice([f"s{i}" for i in range(50)], n),
                   "temp": rng.normal(20, 8, n)})
effect = {f"s{i}": rng.normal(0, 10) for i in range(50)}
y = df["store"].map(effect) + 0.5 * df["temp"] + rng.normal(0, 2, n)
df.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.1, "temp"] = np.nan          # 10% missing
df["store"] = df["store"].astype("category")           # split on categories directly

model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1).fit(df, y)
new = pd.DataFrame({"store": pd.Categorical(["s3", "s7"], categories=df["store"].cat.categories),
                    "temp": [25.0, np.nan]})
print(model.predict(new).round(1))                    # [6.1 1.2]
print(round(effect["s3"] + 0.5 * 25, 1))              # 5.7 (true average for the first row)
takeaways: pandas `category` columns are split on directly, without one-hot encoding
Each split learns where NaN goes; don't fill gaps by default
Give the column the same categories at prediction time
pitfalls: Passing categories coded as integers without declaring them, so they are split as if 3 were 'more' than 2.

quiz.q: How should you pass a 'city' column with 500 distinct names to LightGBM?
options: Map names to random integers and leave them as numbers
Convert it to the pandas category type
quiz.explain: LightGBM's own categorical handling finds good groups of cities without creating hundreds of mostly-zero columns.

concepts.name: Early stopping with callbacks
concepts.summary: Stop training once the score on held-out validation data stops improving, using eval_X/eval_y and the early_stopping callback.
concepts.why: Early stopping picks the number of trees for you and prevents overfitting with almost no extra effort.
concepts.body:
Each **boosting round** adds one more tree. As rounds go by, the error on the training data keeps falling. The error on validation data, rows held aside that the model never trains on, falls at first and then rises again: the extra trees are learning noise. **Early stopping** watches the validation score during training and stops once it hasn't improved for a set number of rounds.

In LightGBM you turn it on with a callback, a function you hand to `fit` that LightGBM calls after every round. Pass the validation data and the callbacks to `fit`:

```python
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_X=X_val, eval_y=y_val, eval_metric="auc",
          callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(50), lgb.log_evaluation(100)])
```

- `lgb.early_stopping(stopping_rounds)` stops when a validation score hasn't improved for that many rounds. By default it watches **every** metric and stops on whichever stalls first; `first_metric_only=True` restricts it to the first.
- `lgb.log_evaluation(period)` prints progress every `period` rounds (0 for silence).
- `model.evals_result_` holds the full score history after training.

LightGBM always reports one metric that matches its **objective**, the loss it is minimising: for classifiers that is **log loss**, a score of how far off the predicted probabilities are that punishes confident mistakes hard. `eval_metric="auc"` adds AUC, a score from 0.5 (guessing) to 1 (perfect) of how well the classifier puts positives above negatives. After training, `model.best_iteration_` gives the best round, and `predict` automatically uses the trees up to it.

Since version 4.7, validation data goes in `eval_X` and `eval_y`; the older `eval_set=[(X, y)]` still works but is due to be removed. Early stopping considers every validation set you pass, so don't include the training data there.

Set `n_estimators` generously with a small learning rate and let early stopping decide. Keep the validation set separate from the test set, so the final test score stays honest.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=6000, n_features=20, n_informative=8,
                           flip_y=0.05, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=5000, learning_rate=0.03, verbose=-1)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_X=X_val, eval_y=y_val, eval_metric="auc",
          callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False), lgb.log_evaluation(0)])

hist = model.evals_result_["valid_0"]
print(model.best_iteration_, sorted(hist))       # 80 ['auc', 'binary_logloss']
print(round(model.best_score_["valid_0"]["auc"], 4))   # 0.9637
logloss = hist["binary_logloss"]
print(logloss.index(min(logloss)) + 1)           # 178: log loss was still improving!
# AUC stalled first and stopped training; use first_metric_only=True with the
# metric you care about listed first if that matters
takeaways: Early stopping is a callback: `callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(n)]`
Pass validation data as `eval_X`/`eval_y`; `predict` uses `best_iteration_`
With several metrics, the first to stall stops training
pitfalls: Adding eval_metric="auc" and not noticing that AUC, not log loss, decided when to stop.

quiz.q: Where is the early-stopping round count specified in LightGBM 4.x's scikit-learn API?
quiz.explain: Early stopping is configured through the early_stopping callback; the old fit argument was removed in 4.0.

concepts.name: The native API: Dataset, train and cv
concepts.summary: Use lgb.Dataset, lgb.train and lgb.cv with parameter dicts for full control and faster repeated training.
concepts.why: The native API exposes every parameter, reuses binned data across runs and is what the wrapper uses inside.
concepts.body:
The scikit-learn classes are a friendly layer over LightGBM's own interface, the **native API**. It works with an `lgb.Dataset` and a dict of parameters:

- `lgb.Dataset(X, label=y, weight=w, categorical_feature=..., free_raw_data=True)` holds the data. Sorting the values into bins (LightGBM calls this construction) happens the first time the Dataset is used, and the result can be reused across many trainings. A validation set should point at the training set, `lgb.Dataset(X_val, y_val, reference=dtrain)`, so it uses the same bins.
- `lgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round, valid_sets=[dval], callbacks=[...])` returns a **Booster**, the trained model itself.
- `booster.predict(X)` returns probabilities for yes/no objectives (there is no separate `predict_proba`); `raw_score=True` gives the scores before the sigmoid, and `num_iteration=booster.best_iteration` picks how many trees to use.
- `lgb.cv(params, dtrain, nfold=5, stratified=True, callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(50)])` runs cross-validation and returns a dict of per-round mean and standard deviation scores; their length is the best number of rounds. `return_cvbooster=True` also returns the fold models.

Parameters use the official names from LightGBM's parameter docs: `objective`, `metric`, `learning_rate`, `num_leaves`, `min_data_in_leaf`, `feature_fraction`, `bagging_fraction`, `bagging_freq`, `lambda_l2`, `verbosity`. Many have aliases; the scikit-learn wrapper's `colsample_bytree` is `feature_fraction`, for example. Don't pass the same parameter under two names.

Settings that affect binning, such as `max_bin`, are fixed when the Dataset is constructed; changing them needs a new Dataset.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
dtrain = lgb.Dataset(X_tr, label=y_tr)
dval = lgb.Dataset(X_val, label=y_val, reference=dtrain)    # same bins

params = {"objective": "binary", "metric": "auc", "learning_rate": 0.05,
          "num_leaves": 15, "feature_fraction": 0.8, "verbosity": -1}
cv = lgb.cv(params, dtrain, num_boost_round=2000, nfold=5, seed=0,
            callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(50, verbose=False)])
best_rounds = len(cv["valid auc-mean"])
print(best_rounds, round(cv["valid auc-mean"][-1], 4))    # 154 0.9952

booster = lgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round=best_rounds, valid_sets=[dval])
print(booster.predict(X_val[:3]).round(3))                # [0.999 0.    0.   ]
takeaways: `lgb.Dataset` + params dict + `lgb.train` -> Booster
Validation Datasets need `reference=dtrain` to share the training bins
`lgb.cv` with early stopping finds the number of rounds
pitfalls: Passing a parameter twice under different aliases, for example colsample_bytree and feature_fraction.

quiz.q: Why create the validation set with lgb.Dataset(X_val, y_val, reference=dtrain)?
options: So it uses the same feature bins as the training data
quiz.explain: Binning is learned on the training data; the reference makes validation data use identical bin boundaries.

concepts.name: Regularisation and tuning
concepts.summary: Tune row and column sampling, L1/L2 penalties and leaf limits in a sensible order to reduce overfitting.
concepts.why: Beyond num_leaves, a handful of parameters reliably trade a closer fit to the training data for better results on new data.
concepts.body:
LightGBM's tools against overfitting:

- **Row sampling**: training each tree on a random share of the rows, which LightGBM calls **bagging**. Set `subsample` (`bagging_fraction`) below 1 **and** `subsample_freq` (`bagging_freq`) to 1 or more. Bagging stays **off** while the frequency is 0, a common surprise.
- **Column sampling**: `colsample_bytree` (`feature_fraction`) 0.5-0.9 gives each tree a random share of the features; `feature_fraction_bynode` draws a new share at every split.
- **Penalties**: `reg_lambda` (L2) and `reg_alpha` (L1) shrink the values in the leaves, both 0 by default; `min_split_gain` asks each split for a minimum loss reduction.
- **Leaf limits**: `min_child_samples`, `max_depth`, `num_leaves`.
- **Coarser bins**: a smaller `max_bin` allows fewer split points, a mild brake.
- `path_smooth` pulls small leaves' values toward their parent's, and `extra_trees=True` picks split cut-offs at random.

A practical recipe:

1. Fix `learning_rate` at 0.05-0.1 and use early stopping.
2. Tune `num_leaves` and `min_child_samples`.
3. Tune `colsample_bytree`, and `subsample` with `subsample_freq=1`.
4. Tune `reg_lambda`, `reg_alpha`, `min_split_gain`.
5. Lower the learning rate (and raise the number of trees) for the final model.

Use random search, or a smarter optimiser such as Optuna (a library that picks the next settings to try from how earlier ones scored; it has a LightGBM tuner), rather than large grids. LightGBM uses all CPU cores by default, so run either the search or the model in parallel, not both.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=2000, n_features=40, n_informative=10,
                       noise=30, random_state=0)
base = dict(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1, random_state=0)

for extra in [{},
              {"subsample": 0.7},                               # no effect: freq is 0
              {"subsample": 0.7, "subsample_freq": 1, "colsample_bytree": 0.7},
              {"subsample": 0.7, "subsample_freq": 1, "colsample_bytree": 0.7,
               "reg_lambda": 5.0, "min_child_samples": 40}]:
    m = lgb.LGBMRegressor(**base, **extra)
    print(round(cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5).mean(), 4), extra)
# 0.9056 {}
# 0.9056 {'subsample': 0.7}                 (identical: bagging never ran)
# 0.9224 {'subsample': 0.7, 'subsample_freq': 1, 'colsample_bytree': 0.7}
# 0.9264 {... 'reg_lambda': 5.0, 'min_child_samples': 40}
takeaways: Bagging needs `subsample_freq` > 0 as well as `subsample` < 1
Column sampling, L1/L2 penalties and leaf limits all reduce overfitting
Tune tree size first, then sampling, then penalties; lower the learning rate last
pitfalls: Setting subsample=0.8 without subsample_freq and believing bagging is on.

quiz.q: You set subsample=0.7 on LGBMRegressor and nothing changes. Why?
options: Bagging is disabled while subsample_freq is 0
It needs max_depth to be set
quiz.explain: Row bagging happens every subsample_freq iterations; the default 0 means never.

concepts.name: Feature importance and SHAP contributions
concepts.summary: Read split and gain importances and compute per-prediction SHAP values with pred_contrib.
concepts.why: Seeing what drives predictions is how you catch bugs and leakage, and why people trust a model.
concepts.body:
LightGBM reports two built-in importances:

- `importance_type="split"` (the default for the scikit-learn wrapper's `feature_importances_`): how many times a feature is used in splits,
- `"gain"`: how much its splits reduce the loss in total, usually more meaningful.

Get them with `model.booster_.feature_importance(importance_type="gain")`, or set `LGBMRegressor(importance_type="gain")` so `feature_importances_` uses gain. `lgb.plot_importance(model, importance_type="gain")` plots them. Split counts favour features with many different values, simply because they offer more cut-offs to try.

To explain single predictions, `model.predict(X, pred_contrib=True)` returns exact **SHAP** values, worked out with a fast method designed for trees (TreeSHAP): one column per feature, plus a last column holding the average prediction every row starts from. For each row they add up to the model's raw output. For a yes/no classifier that raw output is the **log-odds**, the score before the sigmoid turns it into a probability: 0 means 50%, positive means more likely yes.

Averaging the absolute SHAP values per feature gives a reliable overall ranking, and the `shap` library can plot them.

To check how much a feature matters for the metric you actually care about, use scikit-learn's `permutation_importance` on held-out data; it works for any model.

All of these describe what the model uses, not what causes the outcome, and correlated features split the credit between them unpredictably.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=8,
                          verbose=-1).fit(X, y)

split = dict(zip(X.columns, model.booster_.feature_importance("split")))
gain = dict(zip(X.columns, model.booster_.feature_importance("gain").round()))
print(sorted(split, key=split.get, reverse=True)[:3])   # ['bmi', 'bp', 's5']
print(sorted(gain, key=gain.get, reverse=True)[:3])     # ['s5', 'bmi', 'bp']

contrib = model.predict(X.iloc[:2], pred_contrib=True)
print(contrib.shape)                                    # (2, 11) = 10 features + starting value
print(np.allclose(contrib.sum(axis=1), model.predict(X.iloc[:2])))   # True
takeaways: Prefer gain importance over split counts
`pred_contrib=True` returns per-row SHAP values plus a starting-value column
Check with permutation importance on held-out data
pitfalls: Reporting split-count importance as 'how much a feature matters'.

quiz.q: What does each row of predict(X, pred_contrib=True) add up to for a regressor?
options: The model's prediction for that row
quiz.explain: The per-feature contributions plus the starting value add up exactly to the model's raw prediction, which for a regressor is the prediction itself.

concepts.name: Saving, loading and serving models
concepts.summary: Save boosters as text or JSON, reload them for prediction, and keep serving consistent with training.
concepts.why: A model that can't be reloaded exactly by the live system that serves predictions is not finished.
concepts.body:
LightGBM saves models in its own text format:

- `booster.save_model("model.txt")` (or `model.booster_.save_model(...)` from the scikit-learn wrapper) writes every tree and setting. Pass `num_iteration=booster.best_iteration` to save only the best trees.
- `lgb.Booster(model_file="model.txt")` loads it; `booster.predict(X)` works straight away.
- `booster.model_to_string()` and `lgb.Booster(model_str=...)` do the same without a file, handy for keeping models in a database.
- `booster.dump_model()` returns every tree as a JSON-style dict, useful for inspecting the model.

The text file can also be read by LightGBM's command-line program and by its versions for other languages such as C++ and Java. That is why many live systems serve LightGBM models outside Python, and converters exist to ONNX, a shared file format for trained models.

The scikit-learn wrapper can instead be saved with `joblib`, which uses pickle, Python's general way of saving almost any object. It keeps attributes like `classes_` and works for whole pipelines, but the file may not load after you upgrade the libraries, and loading a pickle can run code, so only load ones you trust.

Things that go wrong when serving:

- **Columns** must match training: the same columns, in the same order, with the same dtypes, and category columns with the same categories.
- A loaded `Booster` returns probabilities for yes/no objectives, not labels.
- Record the LightGBM version and parameters alongside the model.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=100, verbose=-1).fit(X, y)
model.booster_.save_model("cancer_lgb.txt")

booster = lgb.Booster(model_file="cancer_lgb.txt")
proba = booster.predict(X[:3])                       # probabilities, not labels
print(proba.round(3))                                # [0. 0. 0.]
print(np.allclose(proba, model.predict_proba(X[:3])[:, 1]))   # True

text = booster.model_to_string()
print(text.splitlines()[0], booster.num_trees())     # tree 100
takeaways: `save_model` writes a portable text file; `lgb.Booster(model_file=...)` loads it
A loaded Booster's `predict` returns probabilities for yes/no objectives
Keep column order, dtypes and categories identical when serving
pitfalls: Feeding columns in a different order at serving time, which silently produces wrong predictions.

quiz.q: You load a yes/no model with lgb.Booster(model_file=...) and call predict. What do you get?
quiz.explain: The native Booster applies the sigmoid for you, so a binary objective gives probabilities.

concepts.name: Objectives, metrics and imbalanced data
concepts.summary: Pick objectives for counts, quantiles and skewed amounts, add custom metrics, and handle class imbalance.
concepts.why: Matching the loss to the problem often beats any amount of hyperparameter tuning.
concepts.body:
The **objective** is the loss LightGBM minimises. Beyond the defaults (`regression` for squared error, `binary`, `multiclass`):

- `regression_l1` (absolute error), `huber`, `fair`: less pulled around by outliers,
- `quantile` with `alpha=0.9`: predicts the value the target stays below 90% of the time, the building block of prediction intervals,
- `poisson` for counts, `gamma` for positive amounts with a long tail of large values, and `tweedie` (with `tweedie_variance_power`) for amounts that are often exactly zero, such as insurance claims,
- `cross_entropy` (`xentropy`): targets that are themselves probabilities between 0 and 1,
- `multiclassova`: multi-class as one yes/no model per class,
- `lambdarank`, `rank_xendcg`: ranking.

`metric` (or `eval_metric` in the wrapper) controls what is reported: `auc`, `average_precision`, `binary_logloss`, `l1`, `l2`, `quantile`, `ndcg`, `map` and more. A **custom metric** in the scikit-learn API is a function `(y_true, y_pred) -> (name, value, is_higher_better)` passed as `eval_metric`.

**Imbalanced classes**: `is_unbalance=True` or `scale_pos_weight=n_neg/n_pos` (one, not both) give the positive class more weight; `class_weight="balanced"` works in the wrapper, including multi-class. As with any reweighting, predicted probabilities come out too high; tune the decision threshold or recalibrate if you need probabilities you can take at face value. Watch `average_precision` rather than accuracy.

A **prediction interval** is a range the true value should fall in, say 90% of the time. Train two quantile models (alpha 0.05 and 0.95) and check on validation data how often the true value really lands between them.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(4000, 2))
y = 5 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 1 + X[:, 0], 4000)        # noise grows with x0
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = X[:3000], X[3000:], y[:3000], y[3000:]

lo = lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective="quantile", alpha=0.05, verbose=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
hi = lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective="quantile", alpha=0.95, verbose=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
inside = (y_val >= lo.predict(X_val)) & (y_val <= hi.predict(X_val))
print(round(inside.mean(), 2))                          # 0.82 (target 0.90: check coverage, quantile models often undercover)

width = hi.predict([[1.0, 5.0], [9.0, 5.0]]) - lo.predict([[1.0, 5.0], [9.0, 5.0]])
print(width.round(1))                                   # [ 4.7 27. ] (wider where noisier)

def mape(y_true, y_pred):
    return "mape", float(np.mean(np.abs((y_true - y_pred) / y_true))), False
m = lgb.LGBMRegressor(verbose=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr + 100, eval_X=X_val, eval_y=y_val + 100,
                                       eval_metric=mape)
print(sorted(m.evals_result_["valid_0"]))               # ['l2', 'mape']
takeaways: Match the objective to the target: quantile, Poisson/Tweedie, outlier-resistant losses
Custom metrics return (name, value, is_higher_better)
Use one of is_unbalance or scale_pos_weight, and expect inflated probabilities
pitfalls: Setting both is_unbalance and scale_pos_weight, which LightGBM rejects.

quiz.q: How can you get a 90% prediction interval from LightGBM?
options: Train quantile models with alpha=0.05 and alpha=0.95
quiz.explain: The two models estimate the values 5% and 95% of outcomes fall below, so about 90% fall between them.

concepts.name: Learning to rank with LGBMRanker
concepts.summary: Train LambdaRank ranking models with query groups, label gains and NDCG evaluation.
concepts.why: Search, recommendations and feeds are judged by the order of items, and LightGBM's LambdaRank is an industry standard.
concepts.body:
Think of a search engine: for each search it has many candidate results and must show them in the best order. In **learning to rank**, data is grouped by **query** (one search, or one user's visit to a feed). Each query has several candidate items with relevance labels, small integers such as 0 (useless) to 4 (perfect). The model learns scores whose order within each query matches the relevance.

`LGBMRanker` uses the **LambdaRank** objective by default (`objective="lambdarank"`). It learns from pairs of items in the same query, pushing hardest on the pairs whose swap would change the top of the list most. You train it with:

- `group=`: the **sizes** of the query groups, in order, for example `[10, 8, 12]` for three queries. Rows must be sorted so each query's items sit next to each other. (XGBoost uses one query id per row instead.)
- `eval_X`, `eval_y` and `eval_group` for validation data, with `eval_at=[5, 10]` to report NDCG@5 and NDCG@10. **NDCG** is 1 for the perfect order and rewards getting the top positions right most.

Relevant parameters:

- `label_gain`: how much each relevance level is worth, by default `2^label - 1`; labels must be below its length (31 by default),
- `lambdarank_truncation_level`: how far down the list pairs are considered,
- `lambdarank_norm`: whether to even out the size of the updates between queries,
- `objective="rank_xendcg"`: an alternative, often faster objective.

`predict` returns scores; sort by score within each query. Split data **by query** when validating (GroupKFold), and score with NDCG per query. Features describe the query-item pair: how well the text matches, how popular the item is, what this user did before.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import ndcg_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n_q, per_q = 300, 8
X = rng.normal(size=(n_q * per_q, 6))
rel = np.clip(np.round(1.5 + X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, 0.6, len(X))), 0, 4).astype(int)

n_train = 250 * per_q                                     # first 250 queries train
ranker = lgb.LGBMRanker(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=-1)
ranker.fit(X[:n_train], rel[:n_train], group=[per_q] * 250,
           eval_X=X[n_train:], eval_y=rel[n_train:], eval_group=[[per_q] * 50], eval_at=[5])

print(round(ranker.best_score_["valid_0"]["ndcg@5"], 3))  # 0.92
scores = ranker.predict(X[n_train:]).reshape(-1, per_q)
print(round(ndcg_score(rel[n_train:].reshape(-1, per_q), scores, k=5), 3))   # 0.939
takeaways: `group=` gives the sizes of consecutive query groups
Evaluate with NDCG@k per query; split by query
Relevance labels must be small non-negative integers (see `label_gain`)
pitfalls: Passing one query id per row as group instead of the group sizes.

quiz.q: For 3 queries with 10, 8 and 12 candidates (rows sorted by query), what is the group argument?
quiz.explain: LightGBM expects the group sizes in order; one id per row is XGBoost's qid convention.

concepts.name: DART, GOSS, random forests and linear trees
concepts.summary: Know when to use LightGBM's alternative boosting modes (DART, random forest, linear trees) and GOSS row sampling.
concepts.why: These variants can add accuracy or speed on specific data, and you will meet them in competition code.
concepts.body:
`boosting_type` (alias `boosting`) and a few related options change how the ensemble is built.

**DART** (`boosting_type="dart"`) uses an idea called dropout: in each round, some existing trees are temporarily left out, so new trees can't simply lean on them. It can improve accuracy on some problems but is slower, and **early stopping doesn't work reliably**, because the older trees get rescaled as training continues. Key parameters: `drop_rate`, `skip_drop`, `max_drop`.

**GOSS** (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling) speeds up training on large data. A row's gradient says how far, and which way, its prediction should move to reduce the loss, so a large gradient means the model still gets that row badly wrong. GOSS keeps all those rows, takes only a random sample of the rest, and gives the sampled rows extra weight so the totals still come out about right. Since LightGBM 4.0 it is set with `data_sample_strategy="goss"` (`top_rate`, `other_rate`), not as a boosting type, and it can't be combined with bagging.

**Random forest mode** (`boosting_type="rf"`) builds independent trees on random samples of rows and averages them, like scikit-learn's random forest, with no boosting. It needs bagging on: `subsample` < 1 with `subsample_freq` > 0 (or `colsample_bytree` < 1).

**Linear trees** (`linear_tree=True`) put a small linear model in each leaf instead of a single number. Predictions can then rise or fall smoothly inside a leaf instead of in steps, which helps when the target changes smoothly with the features. Category columns are still used for splits but not in the leaf formulas, and training is slower.

Start with plain `gbdt` (ordinary gradient boosting); reach for these when you have measured a reason.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(3000, 3))
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + 2 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 3000)   # smooth, linear target

configs = {"gbdt": {}, "linear_tree": {"linear_tree": True},
           "goss": {"data_sample_strategy": "goss"},
           "rf": {"boosting_type": "rf", "subsample": 0.7, "subsample_freq": 1}}
for name, extra in configs.items():
    m = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=200, num_leaves=15, verbose=-1, **extra)
    print(name, round(cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean(), 3))
# gbdt -1.122
# linear_tree -1.083  (leaves fit the linear trend)
# goss -1.129
# rf -2.37            (no boosting: weaker on this task)
takeaways: DART can help accuracy but breaks early stopping
GOSS is `data_sample_strategy="goss"` in LightGBM 4
`linear_tree=True` suits smooth targets; `rf` mode needs bagging enabled
pitfalls: Using boosting_type="goss" from old tutorials; in 4.x use data_sample_strategy.

quiz.q: Why is early stopping unreliable with boosting_type='dart'?
options: Dropped trees are rescaled later, so earlier iterations change after the fact
Early stopping is only for classifiers
quiz.explain: DART normalises old and new trees as training continues, so the model at a past iteration is not preserved.

concepts.name: Histograms, EFB and GOSS internals
concepts.summary: Learn how binning, histogram subtraction and exclusive feature bundling (EFB) make LightGBM fast.
concepts.why: Knowing the internals explains max_bin, the speed on mostly-zero data, memory use, and when these settings matter.
concepts.body:
LightGBM's speed comes from a few ideas in its original paper.

**Binning.** Before training, each feature's values are cut into at most `max_bin` (default 255) bins at quantiles, estimated from up to `bin_construct_sample_cnt` rows (default 200,000). A bin number fits in one byte, which saves memory. `min_data_in_bin` and `max_bin_by_feature` adjust this; more bins mean finer splits and more memory.

**Histograms.** To split a node, LightGBM builds a **histogram** per feature: for every bin, the number of rows and the sums of their gradients and hessians. (The hessian is how quickly the gradient itself changes, the curvature of the loss; together they give each leaf its value.) Building a histogram takes time in proportion to the rows in the node; finding the best split then only scans the bins.

**Histogram subtraction.** A child's histogram equals its parent's minus its sibling's, so LightGBM builds only the smaller child's histogram and works out the other.

**Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB).** Mostly-zero features that are almost never non-zero in the same row, such as one-hot columns, are packed into a single feature by giving each its own range of bins. Thousands of such columns may become a few, which is why LightGBM is fast on sparse data. `enable_bundle` and `max_conflict_rate` control it.

**GOSS** keeps the `top_rate` share of rows with the largest gradients, samples `other_rate` of the rest, and multiplies the sampled rows' gradients by `(1 - top_rate) / other_rate`, so split gains still come out about right.

**Parallel learning** spreads histogram building over several machines: by splitting the features between them, by splitting the rows (each machine builds histograms for its rows and they are added up), or by voting, where each machine first proposes its best features so less data has to be exchanged.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
from scipy import sparse

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n = 20000
cats = rng.integers(0, 2000, n)                       # one-hot of 2000 categories
X = sparse.csr_matrix((np.ones(n), (np.arange(n), cats)), shape=(n, 2000))
y = (cats % 7 == 0).astype(float) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, n)

params = {"objective": "regression", "max_bin": 63, "min_data_in_leaf": 5, "verbosity": -1}
ds = lgb.Dataset(X, label=y, params=params).construct()
print(ds.num_feature())                               # 2000 (original features)

booster = lgb.train(params, ds, num_boost_round=50)
pred = booster.predict(X[:4])
print(np.round(pred, 2), (cats[:4] % 7 == 0).astype(int))   # [0.08 0.08 0.08 0.55] [0 0 0 1]
takeaways: Features are cut into at most `max_bin` quantile bins before training
Histogram subtraction and EFB make data with thousands of mostly-zero columns fast
GOSS gives sampled small-gradient rows extra weight to keep split gains about right
pitfalls: Raising max_bin to thousands for tiny gains while multiplying memory use.

quiz.q: Why is LightGBM fast on thousands of one-hot encoded columns?
options: It converts them to categorical automatically
It uses only the first 255 columns
Exclusive Feature Bundling merges mutually exclusive sparse features into few dense ones
quiz.explain: Columns that are never non-zero together can share one feature with offset bin ranges.

concepts.name: Custom objective functions
concepts.summary: Train on your own loss by returning gradients and hessians, in both the scikit-learn and native APIs.
concepts.why: A business loss (uneven costs, an unusual target) can be optimised directly instead of approximated by a built-in one.
concepts.body:
Gradient boosting only needs each row's gradient and hessian of the loss, so you can supply your own loss as long as you can calculate those two.

**scikit-learn API**: pass a function as `objective`:

```python
def objective(y_true, y_pred):   # y_pred: raw scores
    return grad, hess
lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective=objective)
```

**Native API** (LightGBM 4.x): put the function in the params dict, `params["objective"] = f`, where `f(preds, train_data)` returns `(grad, hess)` and the labels come from `train_data.get_label()`.

Things to get right:

- The predictions passed in are **raw scores**: the plain sum of the trees, before any **link function** (the sigmoid for probabilities, exp for counts) turns them into predictions. For a classification-style loss apply the link yourself. `predict` also returns raw scores for custom objectives, so apply the link to get probabilities.
- Hessians must be **positive**. If your loss curves the wrong way in places, clip them to a small positive value.
- Give a sensible starting point. LightGBM normally starts from the target's average (`boost_from_average`), but it can't for a loss it doesn't know, so pass `init_score=` to `fit` (or to the native Dataset), or accept a slower start from zero.
- Pair it with a custom metric that reports your real loss, so early stopping optimises the right thing.

Check your gradients numerically on a few points: a sign error trains a model that gets steadily worse while appearing to run fine.
concepts.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np

UNDER_COST = 3.0                         # under-forecasting stock costs 3x more

def asym_l2(y_true, y_pred):             # exactly (y_true, y_pred); y_pred = raw score
    r = y_pred - y_true
    w = np.where(r < 0, UNDER_COST, 1.0)
    return 2 * w * r, 2 * w              # gradient, positive hessian

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(5000, 1))
y = 2 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 3, 5000)

plain = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=200, verbose=-1).fit(X, y)
custom = lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective=asym_l2, n_estimators=200, verbose=-1)
custom.fit(X, y, init_score=np.full(len(y), y.mean()))     # sensible start

pred = custom.predict(X) + y.mean()      # raw output excludes init_score: add it back
print(round(float((plain.predict(X) < y).mean()), 2))      # 0.5  under-predicted share
print(round(float((pred < y).mean()), 2))                  # 0.34 (biased upward, as intended)
takeaways: Custom objectives return each row's gradient and positive hessian of the raw score
`predict` returns raw scores; apply the link and add back any init_score
Provide a starting point with init_score and a matching custom metric
pitfalls: Forgetting that predictions exclude the init_score you supplied at fit time.

quiz.q: With a custom objective, what does LGBMRegressor.predict return?
options: Raw scores, without any link function or init_score
quiz.explain: LightGBM can't know your link, so it returns the raw model output; add the init_score and apply transforms yourself.

concepts.name: Performance, determinism and scale
concepts.summary: Tune threads, histogram layout, Dataset reuse, GPU builds and Dask so LightGBM trains fast and repeatably on big data.
concepts.why: On large data, these settings can change training time tenfold.
concepts.body:
**Threads.** `n_jobs` (`num_threads`) defaults to all cores, using OpenMP. Set it to the number of **physical** cores: hyper-threading, where one physical core pretends to be two, rarely helps here. When several models train at once (cross-validation, searches), give each a share of the cores to avoid oversubscription.

**Histogram layout.** LightGBM can build histograms row by row (`force_row_wise=True`, better with many rows, few features or many threads) or column by column (`force_col_wise=True`, better with many features or few threads). By default it times both at start-up; choosing one yourself saves that time and silences the related message.

**Data handling.** Build an `lgb.Dataset` once and reuse it for trainings that share its bins; `ds.save_binary("train.bin")` saves the binned data to disk for next time. `free_raw_data=True` (the default) drops the raw copy once the Dataset is built. `float32` input halves memory.

**Repeatable results.** With several threads, results can differ slightly between runs, because sums are added up in a different order. For identical runs set `seed` (and specific seeds such as `bagging_seed`), `deterministic=True`, and `force_row_wise=True` or `force_col_wise=True`, accepting some slowdown.

**Hardware and scale.** `device_type="cuda"` trains on an NVIDIA GPU (it needs a LightGBM build with CUDA support); `"gpu"` is the older OpenCL version, which works on more brands of GPU. `lightgbm.dask` (`DaskLGBMClassifier` and friends) trains across a Dask cluster: each machine builds histograms for its own rows and they are added together. LightGBM's command-line program and Spark, through Microsoft's SynapseML library, can train across machines too.

Measure first: often the slowest part is loading the data or a too-large `max_bin`, not training itself.
concepts.code:
import time
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
X = rng.normal(size=(100_000, 20)).astype(np.float32)   # float32 halves memory
y = X[:, 0] - 2 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.5, len(X))

ds = lgb.Dataset(X, label=y, params={"verbosity": -1}, free_raw_data=False).construct()
base = {"objective": "regression", "verbosity": -1, "num_threads": 1, "seed": 7,
        "deterministic": True, "force_row_wise": True}

preds = []
for _ in range(2):                                      # reuse the same binned Dataset
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    booster = lgb.train(base, ds, num_boost_round=100)
    preds.append(booster.predict(X[:1000]))
    print(round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1) < 30)      # True
print(np.array_equal(preds[0], preds[1]))               # True (deterministic)
takeaways: Use one thread per physical core and avoid parallelism on two levels at once
Set `force_row_wise` or `force_col_wise`, reuse Datasets, use float32
`deterministic=True` plus seeds for repeatable runs
pitfalls: Expecting bit-identical models across machines with different thread counts without deterministic settings.

quiz.q: Training 8 LightGBM models in parallel on an 8-core machine, each with default threads, is slow. Why?
options: Each model uses all cores, so 64 threads compete for 8 cores
quiz.explain: Default num_threads uses all cores per model, so running several at once oversubscribes the CPU.
